doc.title: "Papa Jack" Laine and Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine Interview, 1960-05-23

title: La Rocca's claimed compositions and joining Laine's band
summary: Russell asks about tunes La Rocca claimed to write; Laine says he learned them from his band, and repeats the Brunies substitution story.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I was going to ask about some more of these tunes, like the Dixieland One Step, they call it. La Rocca put his name on all of those. Skeleton, Django, Fidgety Feet, Sensation. He claims he wrote all of those numbers. Do you remember any of those other tunes?
He wrote all of them numbers?
But he says all of those he wrote.
No, sir. No, sir. After he learned that stuff from us, he did this thing.
When did he start playing with you? Do you know about...
No, I really don't. I really don't. No, I don't.
Oh, that trash on there. That's a funny...

He came around, you know, and wanted to come into rehearsal once again and another, and so everything was all right, you know. Then he come out with us, playing jobs, you know, different jobs, and not pay him just as well as I pay the rest of the men.
See? I see you. It's nice to meet you. So...

Well, he kept on playing until... with me, until this Mardi Gras Day action happened, when he sent little Brunus in his place, Abbey Brunus, see? Now, when he sent Abbey Brunus in his place, of course, I didn't have... I believe it was about two, three bands I had out only that day. Understand? And I never had enough room to make another band to send out, which I had the band ready if they wanted it. Well, I could send it out. See? And Brunus happened to be in Bearville that day, and Rocker grabbed him, put him in his place to play the carnival parade. That's how he played.
